proof:
# A joint center and coupling exchange with exact atom control

Use the probability half-marginals alpha,beta, compact coupling set Pi,
and median map T from `candidate 641c5559a440bf48`. The
original normalized mixed volume is mu, with total unnormalized volume M.
All positive source fibers are full d-dimensional convex bodies. Fibers
of zero volume do not affect any formula below.

## 1. Translate a retained subcoupling and repair its marginal deficits

For h in R^d, let Q_h translate the continuous coordinate of each source
point by h and leave its integer coordinate fixed. Given sigma in Pi,
retain only pairs (p,q) for which Q_h p and Q_h q still belong to their
respective source fibers. Call the restricted subcoupling eta and put
e=1-eta(X times Y). Since the source densities on each fiber are constant,

    (Q_h)#eta_X <= alpha,      (Q_h)#eta_Y <= beta.

The two residual marginals have common mass e. Couple them arbitrarily,
for example by their product divided by e when e>0, obtaining kappa.
Then

    sigma_h=(Q_h,Q_h)#eta+kappa

is a valid probability coupling of alpha,beta.

The median map has the exact covariance

    T(Q_h p,Q_h q)=T(p,q)+h.                              (1)

Consequently the probability target of sigma_h differs from the translated
target of sigma by at most e in total variation, with the convention
||rho-rho'||_TV=sup_A |rho(A)-rho'(A)|. They share the translated target
of eta, and their remaining positive parts both have mass e. This preserves
retained atoms exactly at their translated locations; no smoothing or weak
approximation of an atom is used.

The union bound and alpha+beta=2mu give the uniform loss estimate

    e <= ell(h)
       :=min(1, (2/M)sum_z [|K_z|-|K_z intersect (K_z-h)|]). (2)

The expression is symmetric in h. For h=t v with |v|=1, slicing K_z by
lines parallel to v gives

    |K_z|-|K_z intersect (K_z-tv)|
      =integral_(v perpendicular) min(|t|,length((K_z)_s)) ds
      <=|t| vol_(d-1)(proj_(v perpendicular)K_z).          (3)

In d=1 the projected zero-dimensional volume is one. The identity follows
because each nonempty line slice is an interval, whose overlap with its
translate loses the minimum of its length and |t|. Boundary slices do not
change the integral. In particular ell(h) tends to zero and is bounded by
a constant times |h|, uniformly in direction for a finite bounded family.

## 2. The optimized depth and every finite transport capacity are Lipschitz

Define V(y)=max_sigma depth_(T#sigma)(y) for every y in R^d. The maximum
exists by the compactness and closed-halfspace argument of the preceding
note. Total variation controls every halfspace mass and hence their infimum.
Applying Section 1 to an optimizer at y gives

    V(y+h)>=V(y)-ell(h).

Applying the same argument with -h proves

    |V(y+h)-V(y)|<=ell(h).                               (4)

For any finite unit normals u_i and weights lambda_i>=0 summing to one,
define a transport capacity

    J_(u,lambda)(y)
       =max_sigma integral sum_i lambda_i
                       1_{u_i.(T(p,q)-y)>=0} d sigma.

The very same construction gives

    |J_(u,lambda)(y+h)-J_(u,lambda)(y)|<=ell(h),          (5)

uniformly in the number, normals, and weights of its caps. Indeed its
integrand lies between zero and one, and (1) aligns the retained cap
indicators exactly. The finite dual theorem gives the exact representation

    V(y)=inf_(all finite u,lambda) J_(u,lambda)(y).       (6)

Thus (4) is also the equi-Lipschitz consequence of (5),(6). Continuity here
uses the uniform-volume source marginals, rather than continuity of the
depth of an arbitrary target under weak convergence.

Every median target gives zero mass to the boundary of K=C_z0. Source
points lie in the interiors of their positive fibers almost surely; any
convex combination with a positive coefficient of a full-dimensional
interior point lies in the interior of the corresponding Minkowski
combination, hence in int(K). If a coefficient is zero, the median point
is the remaining interior central point. This argument applies to every
coupling because it uses only its marginals. Therefore V=0 on the boundary
of K and outside K. In particular any positive global maximum is attained
in int(K). The usual continuous centerpoint bound ensures positivity.

## 3. A finite directional optimality statement

Let y_* maximize V and write v=V(y_*). For every h and epsilon>0 there
is a finite weighted cap cost J as above such that

    J(y_*+h)<v+epsilon,
    v<=J(y_*)<v+epsilon+ell(h),
    J(y_*+h)-J(y_*)<epsilon.                             (7)

Choose a finite dual approximation to V(y_*+h)<=v and use (5). Thus these
costs remain approximately active and their original-center transport
problems remain approximately optimized by the chosen globally optimal
coupling, even while their value is tested at the displaced center. Taking
epsilon=o(|h|) gives a directional condition without assuming derivatives,
attained normal infima, or balanced cap normals.

## 4. A residual transport dual for each genuine joint exchange

There is a stronger inequality that keeps track of WHERE the discarded
mass lay. Let (sigma_*,y_*) be a global optimizer of value v. Fix h, and
let eta<=sigma_* be any subcoupling whose translated marginals are
dominated by alpha,beta. This need not be the maximal retained coupling
from Section 1. Put xi=sigma_*-eta, e=xi(X times Y), and define residual
marginals

    alpha_h=alpha-(Q_h)#eta_X,
    beta_h=beta-(Q_h)#eta_Y.

They have mass e. For a unit u put

    b_u=eta{u.(T-y_*)>=0},
    c_u^h(p,q)=1_{u.(T(p,q)-y_*-h)>=0}.

Global optimality says exactly that

    max_(kappa in Pi(alpha_h,beta_h))
         inf_u [b_u+integral c_u^h d kappa] <=v.          (8)

The coupling obtained by translating eta and inserting kappa is legal,
and (1) identifies its retained cap mass with b_u, proving (8).

For every epsilon>0 the finite-intersection and finite dual arguments of
the preceding note apply to (8), including the constants b_u. Hence there
are finitely many u_i and lambda_i>=0, sum lambda_i=1, such that

 sup_(kappa in Pi(alpha_h,beta_h)) integral c_lambda^h d kappa
   +sum_i lambda_i[nu_(sigma_*)(H_i(y_*))-v]
       <=integral c_lambda^0 d xi+epsilon,              (9)

where H_i(y_*)={x:u_i.(x-y_*)>=0} and c_lambda^h=sum_i lambda_i c_i^h.
To derive the displayed form, use
b_i=nu_(sigma_*)(H_i(y_*))-integral c_i^0 d xi.
Each bracket on the left is nonnegative by the depth of y_*.

Thus an optimal joint center/coupling pair forces some finite cap mixture
for which the largest possible replacement cost at the new center is at
most the cost discarded at the old center, less any old active-cap slack,
up to epsilon. This is a genuine two-center transport exchange statement;
it is stronger than merely bounding the total discarded mass by e. It
remains valid when the retained target has atoms on any cap boundaries.

The assertion also covers e=0: the only residual measure is zero. The
finite dual proof never divides by e. No conclusion about gamma_d, radial
structure, or an exactly balanced cap family is asserted here.

## 5. Optimize the repair over an accompanying fiber shear

The retained-coupling construction permits a useful additional parameter.
Translate the source fiber at integer z by

    h_z=h+(z-z0)b,

where b in R^d is arbitrary. For every legal source pair, the integer
barycentric coefficients in the median map cancel the b term. Thus its
target is still translated by EXACTLY h. All the preceding repair and
residual-dual statements apply with these fiber-dependent translations.

In particular the common modulus ell(h) may be improved to

 inf_b min(1, (2/M)sum_z
       [|K_z|-|K_z intersect (K_z-h-(z-z0)b)|]).           (10)

It is symmetric under h -> -h by also changing b -> -b. No minimizer in
(10) is needed for the bound: every b gives a valid repair, then take the
infimum. For an infinitesimal displacement t h, choose the shear t b and
use (3). This gives the homogeneous directional bound

    |V(y+t h)-V(y)| <= |t| G(h),
    G(h)=(2/M)inf_b sum_z P_z(h+(z-z0)b),                (11)

where P_z(v)=|v| vol_(d-1)(proj_(v perpendicular)K_z) for v!=0 and
P_z(0)=0. The same inequality holds for every finite cap capacity J.
The bound follows directly for every b and t, not by interchanging a
minimizer with a derivative or a limit.
